claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist in a simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness of simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi is governed by a lack of significant lattice distortion.
The low strength of simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi is governed by a lack of significant lattice distortion.
The low hardness and strength of simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi are governed by the absence of secondary strengthening phases.
A lack of lattice distortion and secondary phases limits dislocation pinning in CoCrFeNiTi.
Limited dislocation pinning impedes work hardening during deformation.
A small addition of Nb or Al can introduce controlled lattice distortion into CoCrFeNiTi.
A small addition of Nb or Al can promote secondary-phase formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
An added element with a significantly different atomic radius induces lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation motion.
Secondary intermetallic phases or precipitates provide additional barriers to dislocation motion.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion enhances hardness and strength.
The modified alloy will have higher hardness than the initial simple-solid-solution alloy.
The modified alloy will have higher yield strength than the initial simple-solid-solution alloy.
The modification will increase hardness by approximately 20–30%.
Yield strength will increase by a proportion similar to the predicted 20–30% hardness increase.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature under quasi-static uniaxial tension or compression at strain rates of 10^-3 to 10^-4 s^-1.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on the identity and concentration of the added element and on the resulting microstructure.
